annotations.text: 375 — the device goes: she is holding one, and drawing a phone inside a phone is a picture of a picture. The thread plays directly on the panel, which bleeds edge to edge and stacks — thread, then ledger, then the line. The photograph drops out here too and returns further down the page as the section's own image. CTA is full width at 56px.

768 — the columns stack and the panel bleeds edge to edge, which it cannot do on desktop without swallowing the copy. Device left, ledger right, both centred against each other. The thread runs two messages shorter here so the device does not tower over the ledger beside it. Copy holds a 560px measure rather than running the full width, so the headline still breaks where it should.

1280 — the same composition at a tighter measure: copy 500px against a 64px margin, panel bleeding right. Nothing reflows. If the two desktop widths looked different from each other, one of them would be wrong.

1440+ — the media side bleeds to the edge of the viewport and off the bottom. It is not an inset rectangle with a margin on both sides; that reads as a widget dropped onto a page. Its top edge aligns with the eyebrow, so the two columns start on one line and then diverge.

Copy sits in a 540px measure against a 96px margin. The headline breaks in two lines, and nothing is centred anywhere on the page.

Copy is the brief's, verbatim, with three design decisions on top:

— "for her" is set in the serif's italic. It is the only italic in the hero, and it puts the weight on the person rather than the product.
— The moss eyebrow is the one place the second accent appears above the fold.
— "She did none of it." sits under the resolved cards. Four words carrying the whole proposition, in her voice, in the serif.

One primary action only. "Start a gift" stays a quiet text link in the nav so "See the gift" is unopposed.

What every hero shows in the stage is frame 09 — the animation's rest state, which is also the poster image and the reduced-motion still.

The stage is composed to stand with no photograph in it: window light from the upper left, 5.5% film grain, and the thread bleeding off the bottom edge so the frame reads as a crop rather than a box. Shot 01 drops in full-bleed behind it when the shoot lands. The art direction for that shoot is the artboard to the right.

Nine frames, 14.0 seconds, reading left to right in three rows. Each frame shows the state at the END of its beat, not the transition into it — the transition is written in the Motion row beneath.

The three columns inside every frame stay fixed: the photography plate, her thread, and the things around her. The storyboard keeps the plate as its own column so each beat stays readable; in the built hero the photograph sits full-bleed behind the other two. Nothing ever moves between columns. The whole piece is one idea — the right-hand column resolving while she does almost nothing.

Frame 09 is the hero's poster frame, card for card and bubble for bubble. If either changes, both change.

This is the set the hero establishes, and it is meant to be the whole set. Ten colours, two families, three easing curves, four durations, two shadows, three radii, one stagger value.

Every later section — data forward, care balance, the package open state, the six flow steps — is built from exactly this and nothing added. If a section needs a new token, the section is wrong.

Commissioned, not stocked. Every stock library's “new mother” is the exact thing this brand exists to be the opposite of, and one wrong frame undoes the whole palette.

The constraint that matters most is in shot 01: the right half of the frame must be empty room, because the resolved cards live there. That is layout, not styling — if it is not shot that way the hero does not assemble.

Two decisions shape the right-hand side.

The device is sized BY its content — no fixed height, so it can never be half full. That is the whole fix: a shell with dead space in it reads as a pane of glass rather than something a person is holding, and the thread runs long enough to fill it honestly. It holds seven messages on desktop, five on tablet, and none at 375, where she is holding the phone already.

No cards. Three bordered white rectangles with drop shadows is a dashboard, and dashboards are on the banned list. What she is no longer chasing is set as rows of type under hairlines with the detail right-aligned — a ledger, or a receipt. Quieter, more editorial, and the same device the data forward section will need.

The section's job is to explain, plainly, what the mother chooses to share and what is done with it. So it explains — in three numbered steps, in this order: who decides, what is read, what she gets back.

It never argues. A trust block fails the moment it starts reassuring you, because that tells the reader there is something to fear. It makes no case; it answers the question and stops.

Every step leads with its picture, not its words.

01 shows the asking and the one-word yes, so consent is a thing you watch happen rather than a claim.
02 shows the two records as two chips. Two is the entire list, and a short list of real things reassures more than any sentence about safety.
03 shows what came back as the actual messages, in the same bubbles as the hero — a described benefit is worth less than the benefit sitting on the page.

The hardest sentence in the brief is “not with the giver.” The person reading this page IS the giver, and is about to spend money. Telling them plainly that they will never see any of it is the most trust-building thing the section does, so it gets its own block rather than a clause in a paragraph.

The three names carry a quiet dash, never a cross. A cross says something was refused; a dash says it was never on the list. In the motion, the dashed line finishes drawing BEFORE those names appear — the barrier exists before the people do.
